### Spirograph (`lumenary:spirograph`, models this process)

_From: Geometry and a drawing toy; when: 1965 toy, older mathematics; works best on: Pictures with large areas of tone._

A small wheel rolls inside a larger ring and a pen sits in one of its holes. Because the wheel turns faster than it travels, the pen swings out and back in again, drawing loops. The shape depends on the ratio of the two wheels. When the ratio is a fraction of whole numbers, the curve closes after a certain number of turns, so every gear pair has its own personality.

**How it is made, as the model does it:**

1. Scale the ring to 1 and call the wheel’s relative size k, then trace the pen at (1 − k) cos t + h cos(((1 − k)/k) t), (1 − k) sin t − h sin(((1 − k)/k) t).
2. Find how many times around the wheel must travel before the curve closes: the wheel’s teeth divided by the greatest common divisor of its teeth and the ring’s 144.
3. Draw the curve as many short segments, 220 for each turn.
4. Colour each segment by the picture at its midpoint.
5. In the rosette layout, repeat the process in a grid of small spirographs with random coprime ratios and pen holes.

**The maths:**

$$\begin{aligned}x(t)&=(1-k)\cos t+h\cos\!\Big(\tfrac{1-k}{k}\,t\Big)\\ y(t)&=(1-k)\sin t-h\sin\!\Big(\tfrac{1-k}{k}\,t\Big)\end{aligned}\qquad k=\frac{n}{N}$$

_The hypotrochoid for a wheel of n teeth in a ring of N = 144; h = 1.6 k × the pen-hole slider._ (primitives: parametric-curve)

$$q=\frac{N}{\gcd(n,\,N)},\qquad t\in[0,\ 2\pi q]$$

_The curve closes after q turns._ (primitives: parametric-curve)

$$\rho_{\max}=(1-k)+h,\qquad R_{\text{cell}}=\frac{c\,f}{2\,\rho_{\max}}$$

_Scale for a rosette: c is the cell size, f the size-follows-picture factor (0.42 to 1)._ (primitives: tone-mark-size)

**Dials:** `mode` (Layout) = "rosettes" (rosettes, one); `cells` (Rosettes across) = 11 [3 to 16]; `teeth` (Gear teeth (ring has 144)) = 59 [21 to 131]; `hole` (Pen hole) = 80 [20 to 140]; `line` (Line width) = 1 [0.4 to 3]; `size` (Size follows the picture) = true; `paper` (Paper) = "night" (night, cream); `seed` (New wheels) = 1.

**History:** Curves made by rolling circles were studied by Dürer in the sixteenth century and by many mathematicians after him, and the Polish engineer Bruno Abakanowicz built a drawing instrument for them in the 1880s. The British engineer Denys Fisher turned the idea into the Spirograph toy, shown in 1965 and sold in the United States by Kenner from 1966. It has been a classroom favourite ever since.
